background.definition: Gait abnormalities are often due to variations in the normal appearance of the lower limbs or feet. They may be angular or rotational in nature. Common complaints include in-toeing, out-toeing, clubfoot, and developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Many of these conditions are benign and require only observation because they correct spontaneously over time.

list.listitem: Metatarsus adductus: 1/200 to 1/1000 births.
Clubfoot: 1 to 2/1000 live births.

In-toeing and out-toeing prevalence can be seen in the majority of children at various ages, but need to be beyond 2 standard deviations to become clinically significant. This will occur in less than 5% of a normally distributed population.

DDH may be more commonly seen in girls (19/1000), breech presentation at birth (breech boys: 19/1000; breech girls: 120/1000), or in those with a positive family history (boys: 9/1000; girls: 44/1000).
In-toeing can be caused by metatarsus adductus, increased femoral anteversion, or increased tibial torsion.
Out-toeing can be caused by increased external tibial torsion or femoral retroversion, rotational deformities that are the opposite of those seen in in-toeing.
Intrauterine packing due to multiple gestations does not seem to be a risk factor for metatarsus adductus, clubfoot, or other orthopedic deformities.
Metatarsus adductus is a congenital foot deformity, and is not related to uterine packing. It results in a C-shaped convex lateral border with forefoot adduction and can be flexible or rigid.

External tibial torsion is caused by lateral rotation of the tibia, often after four years of age. Femoral retroversion can be seen in young infants with external contractures of the hip. Both of these conditions can cause out-toeing.

Clubfoot is believed to be caused by an interaction of many genetic and environmental factors, and varies in severity. Musculoskeletal and neurologic congenital abnormalities are often associated with bilateral clubfoot.
DDH is often related to poor acetabular development or hips that are dislocated easily in the newborn or young infant up to 3 months of age.

Newborn examination should include examination of the extremities. Metatarsus adductus, talipes equinovarus, and flat feet can be screened by flexing the feet of the newborn and observing for rigid or deformable defects. B

Infants should be examined for developmental dysplasia of the hip at every well child visit until the child is walking well. Older infants should be examined for asymmetric thigh/buttock creases, leg length discrepancies, and limited hip abduction. B
For breech girls, screening ultrasound at 6 weeks or radiographs should be considered at 4 months to evaluate for developmental dysplasia of the hip. B

In-toeing and out-toeing are evaluated through the use of the torsional profile. Most cases resolve spontaneously. Only those beyond 2 standard deviations require observation and potential treatment. C

Clubfoot and metatarsus adductus can be evaluated by a newborn foot exam. Clubfoot is characterized by a "down and in" foot appearance that can result in significant disability if untreated. Metatarsus adductus is characterized by a C-shaped lateral forefoot border, and is a common cause of in-toeing, but will usually resolve on its own. C
Developmental dysplasia of the hips is best diagnosed through the Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers, but specificity is low. Truly "dislocatable" hips are rare, but require a specialist evaluation. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Internal tibial torsion (feet inward), increased femoral anteversion (feet, patellae inward)
External tibial torsion (feet outward), increased femoral retroversion (feet, patellae outward)
C-shaped convex lateral foot border, some in-toeing, seen at birth
Inversion of heel and forefoot, inversion of heel "down and in", present at birth
Limited hip adduction in infants older than 1-2 months, positive Barlow or Ortolani maneuver in newborns

list.listitem: Key historical questions include elements of parental concern, progression of difficulty with gait, tripping, falling or known congenital abnormalities or a family history of significant childhood gait disorders.
Key physical exam features include range of motion of hip, foot and lower limb.
See for typical presentations of common causes of gait abnormalities.

The torsional profile (thigh-foot angle, hip rotation, forefoot alignment, and the foot progression angle) may be measured in children who are walking where there is a concern for in-toeing or out-toeing ( and ). Values greater than 2 standard deviations of normal suggest in-toeing or out-toeing that may need correction. Repetitive examinations are necessary to determine if abnormalities are correcting spontaneously.
There is no clear evidence that universal screening with ultrasound results in improved outcomes in DDH and no consensus on imaging screening.

The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons clinical practice guidelines recommend performing a screening imaging study for infants <6 months old with one or more of the following significant risk factors: breech position, history of clinical instability, and positive family history.
X-rays are useful after 3 to 5 months to diagnose DDH, but later diagnosis limits therapy options.

Newborn: Screen for talipes equinovarus and metatarsus adductus by inspection. Screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip using Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers. If equivocal, repeat exam in 4 to 6 weeks and consider ultrasound (4-6 weeks of age) or radiographs (after 3 months).
Infant: Examine feet and lower extremities, observe gait, and ask about any gait abnormalities at each well child visit.
Toddler (walking): Evaluate gait at well child visits. If severe intoeing or out-toeing, refer to pediatric orthopedist.

tr.td: Congenital forefoot adducted with a convex lateral (C-shaped border)
Observation unless deformity severe and rigid
Moderate = treated with exercises; severe = may require casting before 8 months
Resolves by age 8 in most cases
Feet face inward, patellae face forward
Observe unless torsional profile beyond 2-3 standard deviations, then refer
Sitting on feet, sleeping in prone position may worsen
Significant negative thigh-foot axis and foot progression angle
Feet and patellae face inward, greater internal hip rotation and tripping gait
No treatment unless severe deformity 2 standard deviations on torsional profile, then refer
Out-toeing usually peaks at ages 4-7 years
Usually observed, but mild degrees may persist
Feet face outward, patellae face forward
Thigh-foot axis should be substantially greater than normal 10 degrees
May be seen in infancy because of hip contracture
Greater than normal hip external rotation and positive foot progression angle
Usually debilitating if not corrected by cast or surgery
Uncertain findings may require serial exam
After 3 months, usual presentation is limitation in hip range of motion
Treatment usually consists of a Pavlik harness
Angle made by the feet when the child is walking forward in a straight line. This value is typically positive when the child is out-toeing and negative when in-toeing

Measurement between the axis of the foot and the axis of the thigh when the child lies prone and knees are flexed 90 degrees. This value measures the amount of tibial torsion. Internal tibial torsion values are typically negative, while most normal patients have a small positive value
A convex lateral border and flexible forefoot can be a clue to metatarsus adductus. Similarly a "down-and-in" appearance with involvement of heel and leg suggests clubfoot

Leg abduction will measure internal hip rotation in the prone, 90-degree knee flexed position. Leg adduction will measure external hip rotation and both should be approximately equal. Increased internal rotation suggests femoral anteversion; increased external rotation suggests femoral retroversion
